title: VERIFICATION: run-26 L-01 (dev never executes the cutover mechanics) is FIXED — pull / setDispatcher / setHook / replaceDispatcher now broadcast in the mandated fail-closed order, and the conservation gate is genuinely non-vacuous
severityRationale: Verification record, not a new finding. Severity carried from the entry under test; no severity is proposed for the ledger.
description: The finding claimed setDispatcher / replaceDispatcher / hook.pull() execute ZERO times on chain 31337. That claim is now false, proved from the broadcast bundle rather than from source: parsing broadcast/DeployMocks.s.sol/31337/run-latest.json by the `function` field of each DISPATCHED transaction gives pull=1, setDispatcher=1, replaceDispatcher=1 on BOTH legs (armed 394 txs, dormant 391 txs), against 0/0/0 at the run-26 baseline. Ordering fidelity holds in real transaction order, not merely source order: armed leg tx[355] hook.pull() -> tx[359] hook.setDispatcher(0xdB05A386...4402) -> tx[360] newUb.setHook(0x2B0d36FA...0dd5) -> tx[361] NFTMinterV2.replaceDispatcher(1, 0xdB05A386...4402); dormant leg 352/356/357/358 identically. This matches DeployMainnetPromotionReady.s.sol:148 exactly. The non-vacuity concern the story itself named as its top reward-hacking risk was REAL and is genuinely prevented: hook.mintDebt() read 0 on entry to Phase 7.6 (despite three earlier index-1 mints) and 5015015000000000000 after _accrueIndex1MintDebt, so without that accrual the conservation assertion WOULD have degenerated. The `require(mintDebtBefore > 0, "VACUOUS REHEARSAL: ...")` gate at :1786-1789 exists, executes, and would fire. The recipient's phUSD balance moved by exactly 5015015000000000000, matching price 10030030 * scale 1e12 * ratio 50/100. The story's figure was reproduced independently, to the wei, on both legs.
impact: The cutover ordering whose wrong direction is silent rather than loud is now executed and regression-gated on every local run. The chain also ends fully working: a post-run NFTMinterV2.mint(1, deployer) succeeds (status 0x1) and accrues 5020030000000000000, and the replacement dispatcher carries recipient=BatchNFTMinter, donationSplit=50, nudgeStreamer=NudgeStreamer, hook=the reused hook.
recommendation: Propose status `fixed`. Do NOT auto-apply — this is fix-pending and only a human closes it. Two narrower residuals are filed separately as DEV27-01 and DEV27-02; neither reopens this entry, and neither should be folded back into it.

The recommendation run-26 issued said in terms: 'One index is sufficient to make the ordering executable and therefore regression-testable', and left the index unspecified. The implementation did exactly that. The residual coverage gap (4 of 5 mainnet swaps unmirrored, index 4 entirely) is real and material, but it is a NEW, narrower claim than the one filed — the original said the calls execute zero times, and they now execute — so it belongs in its own entry rather than as an incomplete fix of this one.

title: The terminal privilege sweep bricks `npm run test:fund-user` on every fresh local chain, and the comment on the failing line still claims the deployer is an authorized minter
severityRationale: Proposed Low. A developer-utility script on a disposable mock chain is broken — no assets, no protocol availability, no value leak. It is above QA because it is a shipped, reproducible break of a command the project's own README instructs developers to run, introduced by this change; and because the in-source comment on the failing line now asserts the opposite of the truth, which is what makes it cost time rather than seconds. Not raised further: the consumer sweep confirms exactly one dependent.
description: `_sweepResidualPrivileges` (DeployMocks.s.sol:1917) revokes the deployer's phUSD mint authority as the last transaction of every `npm run dev`. `script/interactions/FundTestUser.s.sol:46` calls `MockPhUSD(phUSD).mint(testUser, phUSDAmount)` inside a broadcast opened at :43 with `AddressLoader.getDefaultPrivateKey()` — anvil account #0, i.e. the deployer — and contains no `setMinter` re-grant anywhere in the file. Reproduced empirically on a fresh chain immediately after a clean `npm run dev`: `npm run test:fund-user` exits 1 with the verbatim revert `Not authorized to mint` (src/mocks/MockPhUSD.sol:48), trace tail `│   └─ ← [Revert] Not authorized to mint / └─ ← [Revert] Not authorized to mint / Error: script failed: Not authorized to mint`. The comment immediately above the failing call — `// Mint phUSD (deployer is authorized minter)` — is now false and will actively mislead whoever debugs this. An independent repo-wide consumer sweep confirms FundTestUser is the ONLY local consumer of the deployer's phUSD grant: simulate-yield.sh mints MockDola (permissionless), MintPhUSD.s.sol routes through PhusdStableMinter (own grant), FullFlowTest.s.sol uses minter.mint, and everything else targets permissionless mocks. However `script/interactions/README.md` points at `npm run test:fund-user` four times (:47, :283, :352, :383 — the last reading 'Fund test user first'), so the broken command sits inside the documented developer workflow rather than in an obscure corner. Story 079 found this, recorded it as Autonomous Decision 4 and Review Issue 1, and deliberately declined to fix it to honour its own single-file constraint; both of its validators endorsed that reading and both recommended scheduling the one-liner. Filing it here is that scheduling, not a disagreement.
impact: A documented developer-onboarding command fails on every fresh local chain with a revert that points at the token rather than at the deploy script that removed the grant. No asset, availability or value impact — chain 31337 mock token, published key.
recommendation: Add the one-line self-grant inside FundTestUser.s.sol, immediately after `vm.startBroadcast(deployerKey);` at :43 and before the mint at :46 — `MockPhUSD(phUSD).setMinter(deployer, true);` — since the deployer remains the token owner after the sweep. Update the now-false comment at :45 to say the script grants itself the right rather than assuming it. Prefer the self-grant over re-exempting the deployer in the sweep: the sweep's declarative end-state ACL is the more valuable artifact and should not be weakened to accommodate a utility script. Optionally symmetric: revoke again before `vm.stopBroadcast()` so the utility leaves the ACL as it found it.
dedupNote: SURVIVES as a new finding. Checked against every already-open dev entry named in the dedup brief: it is not 1e8cc0dc (progress.json pre-broadcast write), not ec29eacd (clean:local stale .ts, wont-fix — different script, different mechanism: a revoked ACL grant, not a stale artifact), and not b8e3d591 itself. Unique contract:function in the run. No collapse.

title: The cutover rehearsal covers 1 of 5 mainnet dispatcher swaps and is not re-targetable to the other classes: `REHEARSAL_SWAP_INDEX` reads like a knob but the helper hard-codes the index-1 6-decimal Uniboost shape, so index 4 — the 18-decimal prime with the BPT custody shift — stays entirely unrehearsed
severityRationale: Proposed Low. Rehearsal-coverage defect on a local-only script: no on-chain asset is at risk and no mainnet behaviour changes. It is a real Low rather than QA because the unrehearsed index is the one carrying the highest-value movement in the cutover (a BPT custody transfer) and a different decimal class, and because the parameterised-looking constant invites a future operator to believe re-targeting is a one-line change when it is not.
description: DeployMainnetPromotionReady.s.sol performs the swap on five indices — 1, 2, 3 (Uniboost, USDC 6dp), 4 (BalancerPoolerV2, USDS 18dp) and 7 (NudgeRatchet) — with pull/setDispatcher/setHook/replaceDispatcher call sites at :1300/:1341/:1342/:1363, :1456/:1519/:1520/:1528 and :1584/:1623/:1624/:1632. Phase 7.6 mirrors exactly one, on index 1. Indices 2 and 3 are genuine duplicates and cost nothing. Index 7's two distinguishing claims are honestly pinned by static assertions (hookTypeId, ratio == 100), both of which execute and pass. Index 4 has NO local mirror of any kind, and it is the index that differs most: its mainnet swap carries a BPT custody transfer old -> new governed by a five-clause safety doctrine and a resume guard (:1385-1420), and its hook `scale` is 1 rather than 1e12 because the prime is 18-decimal USDS. The local rehearsal only ever exercises the 6-decimal branch, so any defect class that manifests only on an 18-decimal prime is definitionally out of reach. Crucially the helper is NOT re-targetable despite appearances: `REHEARSAL_SWAP_INDEX` (:225) looks like a knob, but `_rehearseDispatcherSwap` constructs the replacement as a `Uniboost` (:1805), asserts `rewardToken.decimals() == 6` (:1818), and asserts `require(price < 1e12, "index price is not 6-decimal-shaped")` (:1846) — which would FAIL outright at index 4, where the registered price is 10 * 10**18. Changing the constant alone therefore breaks the run. Note also that `price < 1e12` is a magnitude heuristic with no mainnet counterpart.
impact: The class of defect the local chain can catch is 'a 6-decimal Uniboost swap went wrong', not 'a cutover swap went wrong'. The BPT custody shift — the single highest-value movement in the whole cutover — and the 18-decimal-prime hook-scale interaction remain rehearsed nowhere. The ordering property itself IS class-independent and is genuinely gated, so this narrows the fix's reach rather than negating it.
recommendation: Two options, in preference order. (a) Add a second rehearsal on index 4 in a follow-on story: swap BalancerPoolerV2 with the BPT custody shift mirrored (old.withdrawBPT(new) with the destination asserted, then replaceDispatcher(4)), which exercises the 18-decimal prime, `scale == 1`, and the highest-value movement in the cutover. (b) At minimum, make the existing helper honestly index-1-only: rename `REHEARSAL_SWAP_INDEX` to something that does not read as a knob, or replace the hard-coded `price < 1e12` with a decimals-derived bound (`price < 10 ** (uint256(IERC20Metadata(prime).decimals()) + 6)` or equivalent) and gate the `decimals() == 6` assertion on the dispatcher class. Either way, add a comment stating explicitly which mainnet indices are and are not mirrored, so the coverage claim is not over-read.
dedupNote: SURVIVES. Explicitly NOT collapsed with DEV27-02 per the dedup brief and on independent test: DEV27-01 is COVERAGE BREADTH (which of the 5 mainnet swap classes are mirrored at all; fix = add an index-4 rehearsal or stop the constant reading as a knob), DEV27-02 is ASSERTION STRENGTH within the one mirrored swap (fix = add a live revert probe). Neither fix closes the other. Distinct rootCauseClass, distinct fingerprint.

title: The intermediate-window assertion pins the fail-closed premise instead of its consequence: deleting `UniboostMintDebtHook.onDispatch`'s OnlyDispatcher gate would leave the whole local rehearsal green while the property it exists to protect is gone
severityRationale: Proposed Low. A hole in a regression gate on a local-only script — no live exploit, no asset at risk today. It is a real Low rather than QA because the hole sits in the exact assertion added to gate the one cutover ordering the mainnet script itself calls 'a silent value leak', and because the correct probe is already spelled out in the story's own Implementation Notes step 6.
description: Run-26's L-01 recommendation asked for proof '(iii) that a mint attempted in the intermediate window REVERTS rather than succeeding'. Story 079 Decision 9 substituted a structural assertion — `require(hook.dispatcher() == address(newUb), ...)` plus `(address midDispatcher,,,) = nftMinterV2.configs(idx); require(midDispatcher == oldUb, ...)`. The stated rationale is sound and the story explicitly permits the choice: a reverting call issued while `vm.startBroadcast` is active is recorded into the broadcast bundle and would fail `deploy:local`. But the two assertions restate the SETUP — hook points at new, index still points at old — and then derive the revert by reasoning about a line they never touch: `UniboostMintDebtHook.onDispatch:129`, `if (msg.sender != dispatcher) revert OnlyDispatcher();`. Delete that line in lib/yield-claim-nft and the local rehearsal still passes green, the run still exits 0, and the fail-closed property — the entire reason the mainnet ordering is what it is — is silently gone. Since `UniboostMintDebtHook` is a first-party contract under active development and the hook is explicitly designed to be repointable across swaps, that is not a hypothetical edit. Both assertions currently pass on chain (`hook.dispatcher()` and `configs(1)` read back correctly), so there is no live defect — this is a gate that would not catch the regression it was added for.
impact: Phase 7.6 regression-gates the ORDER of the four calls (which it does well) but not the CONSEQUENCE that makes that order correct. A future change removing or weakening the OnlyDispatcher gate would ship with a green local rehearsal, which is the specific failure shape the rehearsal was added to prevent.
recommendation: Add the live probe the story's own Implementation Notes step 6 already specifies, bracketed outside the broadcast so it is never recorded into the bundle: between `vm.stopBroadcast()` and `vm.startBroadcast(deployerPrivateKey)`, mint the prime budget and approve, then `try nftMinterV2.mint(idx, deployer) { revert("intermediate-window mint SUCCEEDED - fail-closed ordering is broken"); } catch {}`. Keep the structural assertions as well — they localise the failure. If the bracketing is judged too risky inside a `--slow` broadcast, the cheaper alternative is a standalone Foundry unit test in the yield-claim-nft repo asserting that `onDispatch` reverts `OnlyDispatcher()` for a non-dispatcher caller, so the property is gated somewhere even if not in this script.
dedupNote: SURVIVES. Not collapsed with DEV27-01 (see above). Also NOT collapsed with DEV27-04 despite both being 'the Phase 7.6 assertion block does not cover X' on the same function: the mitigations are disjoint (a try/catch mint probe does nothing for tokenIdToDispatcher; a tokenIdToDispatcher require does nothing for OnlyDispatcher) and the failure shapes differ (a behavioural property that a first-party edit could delete vs a state mapping write). Separate mitigation required => keep both, per the dedup rules.

title: The dispatcher swap retires a Uniboost still holding retained prime and never sweeps it — 20.03 USDC locally, a quarter of it created by the fix itself — and the mainnet twin `_swapUniboost` has the same no-sweep shape on live positions
severityRationale: Proposed Low. Explicitly NOT a value leak: recoverability was proved empirically (rescueERC20 returned the full balance), the owner is trusted per Law 3, and on chain 31337 the token is a mock. It stays a reportable Low rather than being suppressed because the consequence is non-obvious — a competent operator would reasonably assume the address-book dispatcher carries the pot — which is the footgun test under Law 3.
description: `Uniboost._dispatch` streams `donationSplit%` of the dispatched prime to the recipient and RETAINS the remainder for a later `pool()` (Uniboost.sol:222-238; split is 50). `_accrueIndex1MintDebt` now deterministically drives one extra index-1 mint on every local run, adding to that retained balance, and Phase 7.6 retires the holder moments later with no sweep and no assertion about its balance. Measured on chain after a clean run: the retired incumbent 0xdbC43Ba45381e02825b14322cDdd15eC4B3164E6 holds 20030020 (20.030020 USDC) — exactly 50% of four index-1 mints at prices 10000000 + 10010000 + 10020010 + 10030030 — of which 5015015 (25%) was created by story-079's own accrual mint; the remaining 15015015 pre-existed the fix. So the change did not invent the residue, it converted a live retained balance on the LIVE dispatcher into a residue on an OFF-INDEX one. The replacement starts at zero retained prime (verified: USDC.balanceOf(new) == 0 immediately post-swap). Recoverability was probed rather than assumed: `Uniboost.rescueERC20(USDC, deployer, 20030020)` against the retired contract returned status 0x1 and left balance 0, and `pool()` remains callable there (poolerAuthVersion(MultiPooler) == authVersion == 1, owner still the deployer). The value is PARKED, not lost. The cross-artifact half is the reason this is worth recording: mainnet `_swapUniboost` (DeployMainnetPromotionReady.s.sol:1443-1538) has no sweep either, and its indices 1/2/3 incumbents are live dispatchers that have been accumulating real retained USDC from real user mints. That magnitude is NOT measured here — `dev` targets a fresh anvil and no mainnet fork was in scope for this entry point — so the mainnet leg of this finding is tagged unverified.
impact: Local: cosmetic, a small residue on a disposable chain. Mainnet (unverified magnitude): after the cutover the retained-prime pot silently splits across two addresses; any pooling automation bound to the address-book dispatcher calls `pool()` on a contract whose retained balance is zero and reverts `"Uniboost: nothing to pool"` until fresh mints accrue, while the real balance sits on a retired contract nothing points at. Recoverable in one owner transaction once noticed.
unverifiedClaims: the magnitude of retained prime held by the mainnet indices 1/2/3 Uniboost incumbents at cutover time
recommendation: In DeployMocks Phase 7.6, snapshot `IERC20(rewardToken).balanceOf(oldUb)` before the swap and, after `replaceDispatcher`, either sweep it to the replacement (`oldUb.rescueERC20(rewardToken, address(newUb), residue)`) or assert it is zero — so the local rehearsal actually exercises the decision instead of leaving it implicit. More importantly, carry the question to the promotion-ready entry point: before the mainnet cutover, read each incumbent Uniboost's prime balance and decide explicitly whether to sweep it to the replacement or leave it for a later `rescueERC20`; whichever is chosen, assert the end state so the pot's location is recorded rather than discovered. Recommend a fork-based measurement of the mainnet incumbents' balances as part of that entry point's audit.
dedupNote: SURVIVES. Unique root cause in the run — no existing ledger entry covers 'a retired dispatcher retains prime and is never swept'. The nearest ledger neighbours were checked and rejected as duplicates: 3c957109 (promotion-ready:broadcast, 'Phase 4d residue sweep can never fire') is a different entry point and a different mechanism (a branch that cannot execute, not a sweep that was never written), and c358427c (uniboost-cutover mid-flight window) concerns mint reverts, not retained balances. Note the finding carries an unverifiedClaims entry for the mainnet magnitude — preserved verbatim for the severity classifier; do not let the unverified mainnet leg inflate this above Low.

title: Phase 7.6 asserts `configs` and both directions of `dispatcherToIndex` but not `tokenIdToDispatcher`, the third mapping `replaceDispatcher` repoints and the one that drives NFT metadata
severityRationale: Proposed QA. No live defect — the mapping is repointed correctly on chain — and the write is unconditional in the same function whose sibling write IS asserted, so no realistic input separates them. It is worth recording only because the surrounding assertion block is otherwise exhaustive and the omission is a one-line fix.
description: `NFTMinterV2.replaceDispatcher` repoints three mappings: `configs[index].dispatcher` (:238), `dispatcherToIndex` old/new (:241-242) and `tokenIdToDispatcher[index]` (:244). Phase 7.6 asserts the first two, both directions, plus price/growth/disabled preservation — thorough — but never reads `tokenIdToDispatcher`. That mapping is what `NFTMinterV2.uri(id)` dereferences to build each NFT's metadata JSON (name/image/description pulled from the dispatcher). Verified on chain that no defect exists today: `tokenIdToDispatcher(1) == 0xdB05A386810c809aD5a77422eb189D36c7f24402`, correctly repointed on both legs. The realistic failure the gap would miss is a future edit to `replaceDispatcher` dropping line 244, after which every index-1 NFT's `uri()` would keep resolving through the RETIRED dispatcher's metadata — a stale but well-formed string that nothing would flag. Note the mainnet script shares the same omission, so closing it here would make the local rehearsal strictly stronger than its mirror (which it already is on `disabled` and `price < 1e12`).
impact: None today. A one-line assertion gap in an otherwise exhaustive post-condition block, on the mapping whose failure mode is silent-and-plausible rather than loud.
recommendation: Add one line to the post-swap invariant block at :1849-1853: `require(nftMinterV2.tokenIdToDispatcher(idx) == address(newUb), "tokenIdToDispatcher did not repoint - uri() would resolve through the retired dispatcher");`. Consider mirroring it into `DeployMainnetPromotionReady.s.sol`'s per-index preservation read-back for the same reason.

title: The dormant leg mirrors mainnet's promo slot but not its address book: `local-addresses.ts` still ships a real, funded MockKendu where `mainnet-addresses.ts` ships `Kendu: 0x0`
severityRationale: Proposed QA. The dormant leg delivers exactly what L-03 asked for — a reachable dormant promo state — and this residual is disclosed in the story's own Concerns. It is recorded so the 'day-one mainnet mirror' claim is not over-read, not because anything is broken.
description: With LOCAL_PROMO_KENDU=false the PhlimboV3 promo slot is genuinely dormant (promoToken 0x0, phase 0, balance 0, rate 0, startPromotion broadcast zero times), which is the mainnet day-one shape and is exactly what run-26 L-03 asked for. But the generated address book is not a mirror: `server/deployments/local-addresses.ts` carries `Kendu: "0x0DCd1Bf9A1b36cE34237eEaFef220932846BCD82"` — a real MockKendu with totalSupply 1.05e24 — whereas the hand-maintained `server/deployments/mainnet-addresses.ts` carries `Kendu: "0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000"`. So a UI developer on the dormant leg exercises 'dormant promotion on a live token address', while day-one mainnet presents 'dormant promotion on the zero address' — the zero-address handling path is still never rehearsed. Story 079 discloses this in Concerns ('The dormant leg is not a perfect mainnet mirror') and rejected blanking the local Kendu address as out of scope, correctly: the Kendu nudge stream legitimately uses MockKendu and gating it was explicitly forbidden. This is adjacent to, but distinct from, ledger entry 3177eed94ecb6218 (mainnet-addresses.ts carrying type-indistinguishable 0x0 placeholders); dedup should keep them separate — that entry is about the mainnet artifact's ambiguity, this one is about the local leg not reproducing it.
impact: The dormant leg is a faithful mirror of the CONTRACT STATE and a partial mirror of the ENVIRONMENT. The UI's zero-address-token rendering path remains unexercised locally.
recommendation: Do not blank the local Kendu address — it would break the nudge stream, which legitimately needs MockKendu. Instead give the dormant leg a way to reproduce the zero-address environment without touching the chain: emit `Kendu: "0x0"` into the generated `local-addresses.ts` when `LOCAL_PROMO_KENDU=false` (a change in `server/generate-ts-addresses.js` keyed off the same toggle, not in the Solidity), or add a third UI-side fixture. Either way, amend the dormant-leg log line so it states which parts of the mainnet day-one shape it does and does not reproduce, rather than the current unqualified 'this is the day-one mainnet shape'.
dedupNote: SURVIVES as DISTINCT from ledger entry 3177eed9, as the dedup brief asked to be adjudicated explicitly. Ruling: distinct. 3177eed9 is about the MAINNET artifact (mainnet-addresses.ts + generate-ts-addresses.js:generateInterfaceFile) being type-ambiguous — a consumer cannot distinguish 'not deployed' from a real address, root cause AnvilDerivedTypeGatesMainnet. DEV27-05 is about the LOCAL artifact (local-addresses.ts, emitted by the dormant leg) failing to REPRODUCE the mainnet shape, so the UI's zero-address rendering path is never rehearsed. Different artifact, different consumer harm, different fix site, and neither fix closes the other. They share only the observable 'mainnet Kendu is 0x0', which is a shared premise, not a shared root cause. Collapsing them would bury the rehearsal-fidelity claim inside an address-book-typing claim and lose it.
